title: Body Doubling for Chores: The ADHD Trick That Gets You Off the Couch
description: What body doubling is, why it makes chores easier to start, and 7 ways to try it today, even if you live alone.
keywords: how to get motivated to clean
intro:
Have you ever noticed that you can clean the whole kitchen when a friend is over, but alone you can't make yourself load one cup into the dishwasher?

That's not a coincidence. There's a name for it: body doubling. It's when having another person nearby (working, cleaning or even sitting there) makes it easier to start and stick with a task.

Lots of people with ADHD swear by it. It's free, it's easy to try, and it works even if the other person is on a screen. Here's how to use it for chores.

sections.heading: Why it works
sections.body:
Nobody fully knows why body doubling works so well, but a few things seem to help:

- Someone else being busy is a gentle cue to be busy too.
- There's a little accountability, without anyone nagging.
- It's less lonely and less boring, so the task feels lighter.
- It anchors you in the present so you don't drift off to your phone.

You don't need to explain any of this to the other person. They only need to be there.

sections.heading: 1. The in-person double
sections.body:
Ask a partner, roommate or kid to hang out in the same room while you clean. They can fold their own laundry, do homework or scroll on the couch. You tidy.

Make it specific: "Can you sit in the kitchen with me for 15 minutes while I do the dishes?" Most people are happy to say yes to something that small.

sections.heading: 2. The phone-call double
sections.body:
Call a friend who also needs to get stuff done. Put the phone on speaker, both clean for 20 minutes, chat as much or as little as you want.

Bonus: you both get a clean-ish house and a catch-up call. That's a two-for-one.

sections.heading: 3. The video double
sections.body:
Search for "clean with me" videos. There are thousands, from real-time full-house cleans to calm, quiet tidying. Play one while you work and match their pace.

There are also livestreamed "work with me" and "clean with me" sessions where lots of people clean at the same time. It's weirdly motivating to know others are scrubbing along with you.

sections.heading: 4. The virtual co-working room
sections.body:
Online body doubling rooms let you join a video session with strangers, say what you're going to do, then work quietly for 25 to 50 minutes. At the end, you share how it went.

It sounds odd, but lots of people use them for chores, paperwork and emails. Saying your goal out loud to someone makes it more real.

sections.heading: 5. The pet double
sections.body:
If you have a dog or cat who follows you around, they count. Talk to them while you clean. Narrate. "Okay, Biscuit, now we're doing the counters."

It sounds silly. It works. Narrating keeps your brain on the task.

sections.heading: 6. Swap houses with a friend
sections.body: Pick a friend and alternate: one week you both clean at your place, next week at theirs. Two people make fast work of a messy kitchen, and cleaning someone else's space is somehow way less overwhelming than your own.

sections.heading: 7. Build it into the week
sections.body:
Once you find a version you like, put it on the calendar. "Sunday 7pm: clean-with-me call with Jess." A standing appointment removes the decision of *when*, which is half the battle.

Pair it with a timer and a short task list, and you've got a whole system.

outro:
Try one version of body doubling this week. Even ten minutes with a video playing counts.
